affordance_in_statement: To prevent antitrust violations, the market regulations enforce a strict density limit on the proposed mergers: for any arbitrary subset of k corporations (where k >= 1), there are never more than k - 1 proposed agreements exclusively between members of that subset. Furthermore, the total number of proposed agreements m across the entire market is strictly regulated to be exactly n - 1.
removal_suggestion: There is no semantics-preserving way to remove this guarantee because it follows from immutable constraints. If only presentation may change, avoid stating the density and edge-count consequences together in graph-theoretic language; embed them in a regulatory certificate or scenario description so the tree structure is not handed to the solver explicitly.

common_affordance: The density condition makes the agreement graph a forest, and the immutable m = n - 1 condition makes that forest a connected tree.

defeated_student_causes.why_failed: Uses a general DSU/Kruskal-style strategy instead of exploiting the unique paths of the guaranteed tree, so its greedy component-merging criterion does not correctly select the minimum subtree connecting all patent holders.

Sorts edges and applies a generic DSU-based greedy selection, which does not correctly enforce that every edge on the unique patent-holder connecting subtree is selected and that all other edges are excluded.

recommended_edit: Re-present the forest and m = n - 1 guarantees indirectly as part of the merger-regulator's certificate, without explicitly naming the graph as acyclic or a tree; however, because these constraints are immutable, this can obscure but cannot eliminate the structural shortcut.
regression_risk: A presentation-only edit may make the problem easier for the already-defeated DSU/Kruskal solutions to recognize as a standard spanning-tree problem, potentially restoring one of them if its implementation happens to handle the resulting tree correctly.
